You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

The roller wheel on my sliding closet door snapped. I've got two 608 skateboard bearings and an M8 bolt I could use. Could I 3D print a new wheel that spins on the bolt? The old one was about 50 mm across and about 16 mm wide.

reasoning:
I'm sizing a 608 bearing wheel, with an 8 mm bore, a 22 mm outer diameter, and a 7 mm width, mounted on an M8 bolt. Two bearings make 14 mm, so the wheel comes to 16 mm wide. Next I want to measure the bolt length, the gap between the bracket arms, and the track groove width, all at once. I'm limited to eight turns, so I'll keep the checks tight.

I'm moving on to the measurements now: checking the M8 bolt, which may differ from the ISO standard, along with the bracket gap and the rail profile. I also want to confirm the bearing's width and outer diameter, since the 21.22 mm reading I have doesn't match the 22 mm nominal I'm using.

I'm weighing the bearing pocket depth against the web thickness so the inner race is clamped by the bracket and the wheel face doesn't rub it. Recessing the bearings about half a millimetre looks like the cleanest option, with the web hole sized to clear the inner race.

I'm weighing a washer spacer of about 1.6 mm on each side, since the washer's outer diameter of 16 mm touches only the inner race and clears the outer race's inner edge. That would keep the wheel face off the bracket, though I still don't know the bracket gap, so I'm adding up the wheel width plus washer thickness to check.

I'm checking whether a 16 mm gap would fit the wheel and washers, which it wouldn't, since 19.2 mm is needed and the gap is unmeasured. I'm considering a few alternatives, like changing the bearing depth or the wheel width, to see which one clears the bracket without relying on a gap I don't know.

I'm now checking whether the web can be thinner, around 1 mm, with the bearings recessed about half a millimetre on each side. Two M8 washers would add 3.2 mm to the clamp, but the 17.2 mm total still has to fit a gap that I haven't measured yet.

I'm settling on pockets about 6.7 mm deep with a 2.6 mm web, so the bearings sit just proud of each face by 0.3 mm. The washers would be optional, depending on how much clearance the bracket actually leaves.

I'm checking whether bearings flush with the wheel face would still clear the washers, since the washer's 16 mm outer diameter stays well inside the wheel face and shouldn't touch it.

I'm settling the press fit at a 22.1 mm pocket, since printed holes tend to come out a little undersized, and I'm adding a lead-in chamfer. Print orientation is next, with the wheel lying flat so one pocket faces up.

I'm checking the print orientation for the wheel: the bottom pocket opens onto the bed, and the web ring between the pockets becomes a bridge over the 22 mm cavity. Since that span stays under the printable limit and the top pocket sits on the web without trouble, I'm treating the orientation as workable.

I'm settling the wheel's flange and profile details as unknowns to set as parameters, and I'm leaning toward solid walls with standard infill. For the bolt I still need a length, so I'm looking at picking a standard M8 size as a placeholder.

I'm listing the joint hardware now: an M8 lock nut on the bolt, with washers on the bracket side. The bolt passes through the bracket arms, and I'm checking which wheel feature the bolt has to clear, which is the bearing bore. I'm also setting the parameters, measured versus assumed, and working out the web thickness from the wheel width.

I'm defining the bearing pocket depth as equal to the bearing width, with a 13 mm hole through the web, and I'll compute the web thickness in code. I'm also planning how to write the criteria: the pocket should contain and seat the bearing, and the coupon will be used to measure the fit.
